vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. this is the second time in a few months that we have had to discuss the situation of the automobile industry in europe in this house. i regret to say that the situation has deteriorated since our last exchange of views. new car sales decreased by 20% and car production by 29% in the last quarter of 2008. this negative trend continued in 2009: in january and february of this year, sales fell by 29% and 18% respectively. they would have gone even deeper had it not been for the successful programmes launched by some member states to stimulate demand. the crisis is not confined to the european market, exports to third countries have fallen rapidly, with negative effects on the european trade balance. the automotive industry is under pressure worldwide. the outlook for the remainder of the year is not promising: total production of passenger cars and commercial vehicles in europe is likely to fall by between 20 and 30%. this means that in 2009 around 5 million fewer vehicles will be produced in europe than in 2007. the negative forecast concerns in particular commercial vehicles, for which a 35% decline in production is expected. the commission, as you know, reacted quickly to this situation. in october 2008, we made initial recommendations to deal with the crisis in the framework of cars 21, including the involvement of the european investment bank and the scrappage premium. at the beginning of january, i agreed with the eu's economic ministers on a joint approach to the crisis, and on 25 february the commission presented a concept which was endorsed a few days later by the european council and the competitiveness council. the answers we give go directly to the main causes of this really very serious crisis. the reasons are: rapidly declining demand, difficult access to capital, liquidity problems and structural overcapacity. these structural overcapacities are a worldwide phenomenon. what we want now is to preserve the integrity of the european internal market, to avoid protectionism and to maintain solidarity among the member states so that jobs in the automobile industry can be saved. i would like to make it very clear that the first thing that is needed is industry itself. we have already created the framework conditions for a future-oriented automotive industry in cars 21 and we are continuously improving them. to put it very clearly, the european automobile industry must now move forward on a broad front to bring to market the cars that are required today at the beginning of the 21st century: energy-efficient, low-fuel and resource-saving. the commission has taken a clear political position. the most important thing, we believe, is to restore the functioning of the financial system so that the high investment needs of the european automobile industry can be financed. and this high investment demand is due to the fact that the european car of the future must now be developed and brought to market. we have adopted the temporary community framework on state aid, which gives member states more room to manoeuvre in dealing with liquidity problems. this was necessary to ensure that otherwise profitable companies did not fall victim to the acute effects of the crisis. we also want to ensure that investment in research and modernisation is continued during the crisis - and especially during the crisis. the measures to this end are far-reaching. the european investment bank has already approved projects for the automotive sector worth more than eur 3 billion this year, with further projects worth several billion euros in total already in preparation for 2009. these projects take into account not only vehicle manufacturers but also subcontractors. the european investment bank - to which i express my gratitude for its cooperation - is also working on a special programme for the supply sector, which has been particularly hard hit by the crisis and is characterised by a small and medium-sized enterprise structure. we will provide one billion euros for research partnerships with industry to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon and energy-efficient economy. this is necessary to give european industry a good starting point for the post-crisis period so that it can really benefit from the positive development that is expected thereafter. there's also something to be done on the demand side. a number of member states have introduced scrappage premiums to stimulate demand. the commission has drawn up guidelines for member states to follow when introducing such support schemes. this is to ensure that national measures do not have a discriminatory effect and do not disturb the internal market. i'm happy to tell you that that worked out, too. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. if the european automotive industry is to remain competitive in the long term, some structural changes will be unavoidable. this process will be painful, but it is inevitable. we need a vibrant and competitive industry with high employment potential and not companies that are permanently dependent on subsidies. the european commission has made funds available through the european social fund and the globalisation fund to support those workers most affected by the temporary effects of the necessary restructuring of our industry. in april we will be holding a first round table with representatives of industry, workers and the member states to discuss the social dimension of the crisis and the response to it. i would, however, recommend that we should promote the continuing training of workers and thus preserve their employment opportunities, whether in the automotive industry or in other sectors of the economy. i should like to say a word about the situation of a particular manufacturer, a word about the situation of general motors in europe with its opel, vauxhall and saab brands. i repeat that it is not in the european interest to let this producer go under! more than 200 000 jobs depend on this manufacturer throughout europe. i do not share the view that the withdrawal of general motors as a european manufacturer would be a contribution to solving the capacity problems of the european automobile industry and as such would be welcome. the workers concerned did not cause the crisis in their company. this crisis has arisen in america alone. there is no national solution to this problem. there is not even a european solution. there can only be a transatlantic solution involving the parent company. and that is why we need to know what is going to happen in the united states. we don't know that today. the american government doesn't know yet. i am pleased that all european governments with gm sites have agreed to abandon national isolation and work together on the european part of a solution. and the only way that solution can be is to end up with a viable, competitive successor company in the market. it must be a solution that is economically justifiable, not just politically. the jobs at general motors in europe are too important to allow them to be dragged into election campaigns or national interest politics. the commission will therefore continue to work with all its strength to ensure that such a european solution is found. finally, the commission will also ensure that its legislative work does not impose any additional and avoidable financial burden on the automotive industry in these difficult times. we can no longer just talk about how bad the crisis is. we have a european plan with coordinated action at both eu and member state level. it is time to act and to put these plans into full effect. thank you, thank you.

say, if there was interest, i would say more about the tripartite, but we agree on three basic principles, which is to allow for much greater labour market flexibility, labour mobility, to work much more intensively on the higher education and skills of the labour force so that it can be applied in the labour market, etc. the spring european council was the second meeting of heads of state that we have held, but it was the first formal summit. perhaps the most widely followed topic was the question of how to deal with the current economic crisis. i absolutely reject the notion that we're doing little, that we're doing little of the deep stuff. i'll give you one number: 400 billion euros. the european union has taken unprecedented steps, and in conjunction with the automatic stabilisers that the european union has and the united states of america, for example, does not, i think that the example that josé manuel barroso gives is quite instructive. the worker who is fired from saab in sweden and the worker who is fired from general motors somewhere in chicago have completely different social standards, completely different approaches of their governments and it is the automatic stabilizers that multiply that amount of 400 billion euros to a much higher one and give us an undeniable advantage in this against the united states. the basic support for this consensus of all 27 is the confirmation of the validity of the lisbon strategy, which is one of the four pillars on which the whole strategy is based. you had gordon brown here yesterday and he certainly had the opportunity to explain to you the approach of the whole 27, the mandate for the g20 summit and in fact the other three pillars of this strategy. all short-term measures, and we agreed that, must be temporary and are intended to be temporary. the medium and long-term priorities and guidelines of the lisbon strategy have been confirmed, and the short-term ones must be aligned with them. i must say frankly that, following the words of timothy geithner, the united states secretary of the treasury, the european council was more or less appalled by the idea of permanent action. not only is america repeating the mistakes of the 1930s, but there are widespread incentives, trends and calls for protectionism, the buy american campaign and so on. all these steps, their combinations, and worse, the initiative for their permanent establishment, are the road to hell. you have to read the history books, which have obviously been dusted. i consider the most important achievement of the spring council meeting to be the clear rejection of this path and this short-sighted approach. i must firmly reject the words of the president of the party of european socialists, poul nyrup rasmussen, that we in the european council have done little to combat the crisis and that we are waiting for a bailout from the united states. not only because the path chosen by the us has already historically discredited itself, but also because, as i said, the level of social security and the provision of social needs of citizens in general is significantly different in the us and at a significantly lower level. that's why the dangerous part of this path is that to fund their social incentives, americans will need cash, and they'll get it easily, because american bonds are always bought. but it will threaten the liquidity of the market, it will take liquidity out of the global financial market and in the case of other bonds, maybe european, but certainly polish, czech, maybe other countries, their sale will be threatened and then there will be no cash in the system. this approach is a concern and i think it will be discussed at the g20 summit. the g20 summit will be one of the opportunities to talk about this. the informal 27th summit with the us administration and barack obama in prague may be a continuation of this discussion. i believe that the united states and i will find a common solution, because we do not want to set america and europe against each other. today, and this crisis has shown us again and again, that there is no such thing as an isolated economy, and the degree of interconnectedness is very high, which means that in times of crisis, we all have a problem, and we can only solve it together. the second pillar of the consensus on finding a solution to the current crisis is the preparation of the g20 summit. the materials that gordon brown has prepared with his administration are excellent and you had the opportunity to see them yesterday. the three-pillar approach, which means dealing with the financial sector and fiscal incentives, regulation and i would say correcting the errors within that system and the renewal and liberalisation of world trade, which means pushing for the resumption of the doha negotiations within the wto, is exactly what i believe is a certain set of solutions that the european council is offering and on which it has unambiguously agreed. i would also like to point out that we finally agreed on a specific figure for increasing the available financial capacity of the international monetary fund, and we defined this specific commitment at 75 billion euros. the 27 have a common position, a single voice and a common objective in the g20. i considered this to be the greatest achievement of all, because this whole european council was a test of european unity, european solidarity, european values and the european single market. if any of this is compromised, we'll actually come out of this crisis weakened. and i think, on the contrary, that if we respect these basic attributes, we will come out stronger. there is no reason to be pessimistic about the g20 as mr rasmussen is concerned, and i think we all understand the need for solidarity and cooperation, as graham watson of the liberal group has said. the current crisis, as we all say, is a crisis of trust. the third area, therefore, which is key to resolving the crisis, is the restoration of trust. it's not enough to just pour money into the system. we tried that, and the banks still won't lend money. the banks need to lend this money. and banks won't do that until they have confidence. the liquidity they have at their disposal hasn't solved the problem. trust can neither be commanded nor bought. so as part characterised these early contacts. while the change of tone is important, it does not of course in itself deliver concrete outcomes. if we are to work constructively together we must review together our policy priorities, and reassess the way in which the transatlantic partnership functions. your report is a valuable contribution to that process. it is, of course, a process which began on the eu side last year when the foreign ministers discussed transatlantic relations at the two informal meetings in avignon and marseille. i think some thanks are due here both to the french presidency for initiating that and to portugal, which also played a role. it is a process which will need to continue to be developed over the coming months. an excellent opportunity will present itself next week at the informal meeting of heads of state and government with the us president in prague. the transatlantic relationship is rich and varied and includes a number of policy areas. i cannot touch on all of them but i would like to highlight those that we would like to address in particular at the forthcoming meeting in prague. firstly, energy security and climate change. these interconnected topics are of concern to a great many europeans. energy security is a key priority which needs to be pursued via a comprehensive strategy covering energy efficiency and the promotion of renewable energy resources as well as the diversification of energy supplies, sources and routes. wherever possible and necessary the eu and us should cooperate in these areas and promote a common agenda. on climate, this year will be critical. the united nations climate change conference in copenhagen in late december presents a historic opportunity to revise and widen the application of binding international targets to address climate change. the eu has established ambitious energy and climate change commitments in advance of the conference. president obama’s statements and appointments in relation to climate change appear to signal an important policy shift, but much hard work lies ahead here. of course, support from the us on this issue is vital, but it is not enough. we must also secure backing from advanced developing countries such as china. secondly, the economic and financial crisis. the current crisis is both severe and global and requires a strong policy response at all levels and across the world. the eu and the us have a particular responsibility in this context, both in terms of the measures they take at home and in terms of international coordination. we must cooperate with the us to ensure that we deliver a coordinated response to the current global crisis and financial problems. we must work together to address the issue of the supervision of the financial system and the reform of international financial institutions. we must also coordinate our policies for enhanced growth and employment. we must make sure that the approaches we choose are compatible and do not give rise to distortions of competition in the transatlantic market place. much of this will take place in groups such as the g8 and g20, in particular during the g20 summit in london with which president obama’s visit to europe will start. but it is clear that the transatlantic relationship will be key in setting the wider global agenda. thirdly, afghanistan is a key issue for both europe and the us. this is a joint problem – terrorist attacks in both the us and europe have their origins in the region. it is an important, and uneasy, challenge for all european political leaders to explain to their citizens that their own security must be defended in kabul. afghanistan was also the main subject of an informal meeting of the eu troika with vice-president biden in brussels on 10 march. the vice-president expressed the hope that afghanistan would remain at the top of the eu agenda. he was clear that the us was looking not just for our support for the overall strategy in afghanistan, but also for commitment to match that support with concrete resources. knowing that the question of security of afghan citizens is of major concern, we have undertaken to increase the size of our police mission in the country. in addition to the eupol civilian mission, military police are needed, the ‘gendarmeries’ which we are talking about. in this respect, sending gendarmerie trainers on site, as an eu contribution to the nato mission, is an option which the presidency has been discussing with the freshly appointed special envoy for pakistan and afghanistan amongst eu countries. i have met pierre lellouche from france, for example, and we are also discussing this with dick holbrooke. we must also ensure that the conditions are in place for the presidential elections in afghanistan to be a success and we must keep the regional aspect in mind, in particular by giving further assistance to the development of sustainable civil government in pakistan. so this regional dimension is very important and we are taking account of this in addition to the national dimension and then the global one. fourthly, a multilateral response will be crucial to address to act against them. and that this is not a second arm, so to speak, which is created to fight cartels on an equal footing with the authorities. we in europe have consciously chosen a different path from that of the united states, with which the situation is often compared. there is a political consensus in this house that there must be a solution to the so-called mass phenomenon. if a very large number of individuals are harmed by unlawful conduct, but suffer comparatively little damage, then something special is needed for those proceedings where ordinary procedural procedures are simply not effective enough. and it is also part of access to justice and the further development of the internal market that such a tool is being created. there is a consensus on this. but there was also a consensus that we do not want europe to become a litigation industry, as we know it in america, with a turnover of 240 billion dollars, where the end result is not usually the consumer, but - and we strongly criticise this - to deal with the issue of out-of-court dispute settlement. the directorate-general for competition and the commission are moving swiftly towards legal proceedings. but we know from the debate on legal policy in this house over many years that this is not always the ideal way, and that as a rule, out-of-court dispute settlement mechanisms are often much more appropriate to solve problems. the parallel work of the directorate-general for consumer protection on the same subject has, incidentally, gone much further. in its green paper, the directorate-general has made a wide use of these alternative dispute resolution instruments, i.e. a consultation phase. we believe that it is imperative that the european commission should continue to work on this issue. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the creation of such an instrument is now under way in competition law. consumer protection is the same issue. we know that at some point similar considerations will be made in the area of capital market law, environmental law and social law. we believe it is imperative that a horizontal approach should also be considered and that at least the procedural instruments, which are more or less the same in all areas, should be used with a horizontal instrument. this is also of crucial importance.

member of the commission. − mr president, since the beginning of my mandate, redress has, as you know, been high on my list of priorities. i believe that substantive rights show their strength only when they are backed by enforcement and effective redress for consumers. more and more often, large numbers of consumers lose out as a result of the same or similar illegal practices by a trader and do not receive redress. the commission has been examining the problem that consumers face in obtaining redress for mass claims. we have commissioned studies, discussed the issue with stakeholders, conducted surveys and an internet consultation, and recently published a green paper to which we have received more than 170 responses. although the consultation officially ended on 1 march 2009, comments are still coming in and i can already tell you that, the more evidence we gather, the more our belief that there is a problem is confirmed. this is why we need to find a solution in the interests of justice and a healthy european economy. the green paper on consumer collective redress proposed various ways of tackling this problem. a preliminary analysis of the replies received indicates that stakeholders recognise the unsatisfactory present situation on collective redress in the member states. there is consensus about the necessity of further action to achieve effective redress for consumers and thereby restore their confidence in the market. consumer organisations favour binding measures for a collective redress judicial scheme in all member states in combination with other options, such as the extension of existing alternative dispute resolution (adr) mechanisms to collective claims. business would favour adr mechanisms. in a few weeks’ time, once we have properly analysed all the responses, we will publish the replies, together with a statement on the feedback we received, and before the summer we will outline the different ways of addressing the problem of mass claims. this will not simply be a repetition of the four options in the green paper. our thinking is developing further in the light of the responses to the green paper consultation. based on the outcome of all the consultations, the commission will carefully examine the economic and social impact on stakeholders, including the costs and benefits generated by the possible options. on 29 may we will hold a hearing to share our preliminary conclusions with stakeholders. let me stress that, whatever route we take, we will not go down the path of the us experience. instead, we will follow our european legal cultures and take into account the existing experiences of member states. once the options become clear, the european parliament, member states and stakeholders will be convinced, as i am, that not only is there a problem but also that an effective solution must, and can, be found at european level. why should reputable businesses suffer at the hands of unfair competitors who profit when consumers are not compensated? and i stress ‘compensated’. this is the very nature of redress that we are aspiring to. why should consumers give up their legitimate expectations of compensation, and why should society put up with the welfare and justice gap? i am confident that we will find a solution that strikes the right balance between improving consumer access to redress and avoiding unfounded claims. effective redress will boost consumers’ confidence in the internal market and in what europe can do for them. this is particularly important in the harsh reality of today’s economic and financial crisis. as you know, the coming months will be marked by many institutional changes, and this may influence the timing and the delivery of our work on collective redress. concerning the initiative taken by the commission on damages actions for breach of the european anti-trust rules, i can assure you that the commission shares parliament’s view that these two initiatives related to collective redress should be consistent. indeed, being consistent does not mean that different policy initiatives have to use the same tools to reach the same goals. i can equally assure you that i remain personally committed to this issue and will continue to work on it until the end of my mandate with the same energy and vigour that i have devoted to it thus far, and of course with the kind help and support of parliament.

member of the commission. − mr president, nuclear safety is an absolute priority for the european union, as the rapporteur said, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for a very strong, clear and comprehensive report. as the use of nuclear energy in the european union is a reality and will be a reality, and nuclear safety is not constrained by national borders, we need a community-wide framework aiming at achieving, maintaining and continuously improving nuclear safety in the european union. this is the objective of the revised proposal for a directive that sets up a community framework for nuclear safety. the fundamental goal of the proposal is to establish binding legislation, the only solution that offers guarantees that political and industrial commitments to continuously improve nuclear safety are followed by concrete measures. these international atomic energy agency (iaea) safety fundamentals and the obligations of the convention of nuclear safety constitute the core of the directive. de facto, their transposition into binding community legislation would bring legal certainty. the proposal also aims at ensuring that national regulatory authorities in charge of nuclear safety are independent from any governmental decision-making body and any other organisation that would have an interest in nuclear matters. they can, therefore, preoccupy themselves solely with the safety of installations. the proposal aims to enhance the role of regulatory authorities by ensuring that the member states provide them with adequate authority, competence and human and financial resources to fulfil their responsibilities. the revised proposal takes into account the outcome of a consultation process that started in 2004 with the council’s working party on nuclear safety. it was discussed, before adoption, with the european nuclear safety regulators group, as well as in other fora. it also reflects the substance of the opinion given by the scientific group of experts, referred to in article 31 of the euratom treaty, and the current nuclear safety proposal is a second revision of the regional proposal in the area of nuclear safety. article 31 of the euratom treaty does not require a resubmission of the revised proposal to the scientific group of experts. moreover, close cooperation with the international atomic energy agency has ensured consistency with international practices. the commission agrees with most of the proposed amendments that reinforce the line taken. the report clearly recognises the obligation of the member states to respect the safety fundamentals stemming from the iaea and the provisions of the convention on nuclear safety, as well as seeking to reinforce the role of nuclear regulatory authorities and ensure their independent decision-making role. i am, therefore, confident that the council will take into consideration parliament’s position whenever it contributes to improving and clarifying the objectives of the directive.

member of the commission. − madam president, today’s debate takes place at a time when we are facing the greatest challenge to the european economy in modern times. action is needed urgently: vigorous, targeted and comprehensive action in order to restore confidence, growth and jobs and to repair the financial system, to rebuild stability for the future, to promote trade and investment and to better protect our citizens – in short, to deliver an effective and stable financial system. based on the commission’s communication of the beginning of march, the spring european council set out a strong eu action plan for the future – a strategy to address the regulatory gaps in the financial sector, to restore incentives and to reform supervision to match the single eu financial market. in a few weeks’ time the commission will present its views on the road towards building a state-of-the-art supervisory framework in europe. these will be discussed by the heads of state or government in june. the commission is ready to put concrete measures on the table in the autumn. clearly, global problems also require global solutions. the eu initiative to agree a coordinated global response to the financial crisis has been very successful. at the london meeting, g20 leaders made extensive commitments to address the weak points of the financial system in a coordinated manner, to jointly build a new financial architecture while defending an open, global economy. the situation in the eu financial sector is serious. but a lot has already been done, and i am glad to note that the commission, the european parliament and the council have reacted quickly and cooperated closely to respond to the crisis. we are about to successfully conclude the adoption of three key measures: firstly, the regulation on credit-rating agencies; secondly, the recast of solvency ii, as well as, thirdly, the revision of the third and sixth company law directives on domestic mergers and divisions. firstly, the agreement reached on a regulation on credit-rating agencies will help address one of the problems that contributed to this crisis and thus will offer some prospect of restoring market confidence. the proposal adopted by the commission last november sets some clear objectives for improving integrity, transparency, responsibility and good governance of the credit-rating agencies. the thrust of the initial proposal is preserved in this regulation, which will in particular secure the analytical independence of credit-rating agencies, the integrity of the rating process and an adequate management of conflicts of interest that existed before in the rating process. moreover, a comprehensive supervisory regime will be put in place. european regulators will supervise the conduct of credit-rating agencies and take enforcement action where necessary. on the issue of supervision, i have been vocal about the need to strengthen supervisory cooperation. i have therefore no difficulty in agreeing on the need to push forward in this crucial domain. therefore, in order to ensure consistency and coherence in all relevant financial sector regulation, the commission agrees, on the basis of the recommendations of the de larosière report, to examine the need to strengthen the provisions of this regulation with regard to supervisory architecture. on the issue of the treatment of credit ratings issued in third countries, the outcome of the g20 summit has changed the global situation. all g20 members have agreed on regulating credit-rating agencies through the introduction of mandatory registration and oversight regime. that is why i agree with the solution agreed in the negotiations between the council and parliament on the treatment of ratings issued in third countries. i am pleased to note that the ambitious goals set by the commission proposal have been kept. the commission is very pleased with the outcome of the codecision process. let me now turn to solvency ii. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr skinner, and parliament for their work and their willingness to compromise in order to reach agreement in a single reading on this important subject. such an outcome will be widely welcomed by the eu insurance industry, by supervisors and by stakeholders in general. however, i also have to admit that i am disappointed with certain aspects of the compromise. the deletion of the group support regime, which i consider one of the most innovative aspects of the commission’s proposal, means that we will not be able to modernise – as much as we wanted – the supervisory arrangements for insurers and reinsurers operating on a cross-border basis. i also remain concerned that some of the amendments regarding the treatment of equity risk could result in the introduction of an imprudent regime for investment in risk-based capital. this is particularly the case for the amendments which introduce the so-called duration approach as a member state option. the commission will pay close attention to ensure that the implementing measures brought forward in this regard are prudentially sound. nonetheless, the commission will support the agreement between parliament and the council, if it is endorsed by your vote. the current solvency regime is over 30 years old. solvency ii will introduce an economic risk-based regime that will deepen integration of the eu insurance market, enhance policyholder protection and increase the competitiveness of eu insurers. as confirmed recently by ceiops in their report on lessons learned from the financial crisis, we need solvency ii more than ever as a first response to the present financial crisis. we need regulation that requires companies to properly manage their risks, that increases transparency and that ensures that supervisory authorities cooperate and coordinate their activities more effectively. solvency ii will bring about a regime for the insurance industry that can serve as a model for similar reforms internationally. the introduction of a review clause specifically mentioning the group support regime will enable the commission to come back to this issue. i expect that progress in a number of different areas, connected to the recommendations of the de larosière report, will have created a more favourable environment for reforms related to cross-border cooperation between home and host supervisors. i now turn to the weber report. thanks to the efficient work of the rapporteur, ms weber, it has been possible to identify a compromise on simplified reporting and documentation requirements, in the case of mergers and divisions of public limited liability companies which will maintain a very significant part of the savings potential of the original commission proposal, which amounts to eur 172 million per year. measurements and studies carried out in the context of reduction of administrative burdens show that company law is one of the most burdensome areas of the eu acquis. for several reasons, administrative burdens hit smes harder than bigger companies. an expert report from 2007 estimates that small enterprises spend 10 times the amount that large enterprises have to spend in order to comply with information obligations imposed by legislation. ten times, i repeat. at the same time, small businesses are the backbone of our i am sorry, but i have to say that i am not in favour of the amendments. the commission has already made a number of proposals. just as public security, justice or environmental protection, the stability of financial markets is a public good and should be publicly controlled. we 've seen it . if you leave the regulation of financial markets to the private sector, to big banks, insurance companies, hedge funds and rating agencies, you risk the risk of speculating huge sums in the search for maximum returns and, in the end, the general public having to pay for the losses. the crisis has shown all too clearly that voluntary self-regulation has failed. the commission is nevertheless firmly committed to this. instead of banning risky financial products and setting clear rules for the financial sector, private players should be able to decide for themselves what risks they take and how to assess them. we think that's irresponsible. it is now clear that the rating agencies, in the interest of profit, systematically underestimated the risks of structured finance products and thus really started trading in bad debt securities. it would therefore be appropriate to end the outsourcing of risk management to private, profit-oriented actors altogether and to create a public european rating agency that can independently assess the quality of different securities. the commission has not even considered this solution. the gauzès report rightly calls for the rating of sovereign debt to be regarded as a public task and therefore to be undertaken by public actors. but why should this principle apply only to government bonds? the commission and the rapporteurs also rely on the failed concept of self-regulation in the proposed solvency ii directive; for example, insurance groups should be allowed to use internal risk assessment models for the calculation of solvency and capital requirements. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and to monitor the implementation of the new rules. i personally doubt that. in addition, both the capital requirements and the solvency capital requirements are far too low. you need to raise them up a little bit. since this could cause problems for some banks or insurance companies, we advocate that such an increase in equity capital be achieved through public participation, which is linked to an appropriate influence on business policy. such partial nationalisation would be a bold first step towards reorienting the financial sector towards the public good. in the longer term, the entire financial sector should be taken over by the public sector anyway. this is the only way to ensure that the financial sector fulfils its public mandate, rather than seeking ever higher returns on the global financial markets. it is really time to draw lessons from the catastrophe that has been wrought.

of this body of legislation to be of great importance. this package is important in view of the need for a clear and harmonised approach due to the different practices in the member states regarding the use of the existing cabotage system, as well as in view of the approach of operators to the transport sector. with the support and assistance of the rapporteurs, the bureau has succeeded in achieving a successful outcome on this important body of legislation. i know that everyone has made a great effort to achieve this result and that everyone has had to make certain compromises. during the negotiations, all showed a constructive approach with a view to reaching an agreement at second reading. the main elements of our discussions can be summarised as follows: more precise rules on cabotage, the possibility for coach drivers in occasional international transport to work 12 consecutive days and stricter controls on transport companies. the road transport sector can now quickly benefit from simplified cabotage rules and control mechanisms, as well as from uniform and enforceable provisions for access to the transport sector. this also means that there will be clear rules to sector. the number of empty vehicle journeys on community roads will be reduced, thus contributing to the reduction of co2 emissions. the compromise also provides that member states shall use appropriate safeguards to prevent disturbances in the road haulage market caused by cabotage. the new cabotage rules shall apply six months after the publication of the regulation in the official journal. the european commission will also assess in 2013 the possibility of further steps concerning the possible opening of the road transport market and the liberalisation of cabotage. i am conditions imposed by the undertakings competing in that market. this is the aim of the new regulation which replaces a directive which at the same time makes the conditions which companies must meet more stringent. each undertaking will have to appoint a transport manager, responsible for the smooth running of the whole undertaking. in addition, to avoid so-called shell companies, greater guarantees will have to be provided with regard to the location of companies. a new electronic register will also be developed to enhance the exchange of information between national authorities and to make checks smarter and more efficient. here again we are in the complementary field of road safety. finally, transport companies are now receiving a very clear message from the legislator about countries of the european union, but the manipulation is not only a violation of the rules, but it also endangers the safety of those who travel on the roads of the european union, because it is important for the development of rail freight transport. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr duchamp, and the committee on transport for the availability and quality of the work they have done, which has helped to support a legislative proposal which aims first of all to integrate rail transport better at european level through closer cooperation between infrastructure managers. rail transport is the last, and i repeat the last, mode of transport which has retained a strongly national dimension. very often crossing borders by train is still difficult. infrastructure managers are largely responsible for this difficulty and their cooperation must be encouraged, both in infrastructure management and in planning and implementing investment. europeanization of infrastructure is necessary for goods which already have a significant international dimension. i should like to remind you that 50% of freight services are now international and that this figure is likely to increase in the future. secondly, the proposal is intended to allow the development of rail freight services. this sector will not be able to develop and compete with and/or complement the road sector without a considerable improvement in the infrastructure made available to freight trains. today, in a large majority of member states, rail freight is considered an adjustment variable compared with passenger transport. unfortunately, this is true for infrastructure management as much as for investment. thirdly, this proposal will make it possible to integrate railways more closely into the freight transport system and develop co-modality in europe. in order for rail transport to make a substantial contribution to the community's transport objectives, rail infrastructure needs to be better connected to other modes of transport, in particular to maritime and road transport. but in addition to the main objectives of the proposal, i would like to mention four essential principles on which the text we are discussing is based. the first principle is the identification of the corridors and therefore of the network. this is based on economic rather than political considerations. the second principle is enhanced cooperation between infrastructure managers. the third principle, on which i would like to dwell for a moment, concerns the best guarantees in terms of quality and reliability of the services provided by the infrastructure through provisions aimed at achieving a better balance between passenger traffic and freight traffic in the management of the infrastructure. this does not mean systematically giving priority to freight trains over passenger trains on the entire national network. on the contrary, and i would like to stress this concept in particular, on freight-oriented corridors, that is to say on specific and clearly identified lines, this means not systematically disadvantaging freight trains, particularly those with higher demands on speed and/or punctuality. this is, in our view, the most concrete translation of the definitions of a freight-oriented corridor or a competitive freight corridor. finally, fourth point, fourth pillar: the definition and establishment of a genuine network of strategic terminals. in this case the term terminal is understood in the broadest sense: railway stations, port terminals, logistics platforms, roads, railways, etc. which are essential for the smooth functioning of the freight corridor and the transport system in which they are located. that is what i wanted to say when i thank you again for in writing. - the european parliament voted today on the report by mr casaca on the discharge to be given to the european parliament in respect of the implementation of its budget for the financial year 2007. the report also dealt with the european parliament's pension fund. the european parliament's pension fund is a voluntary pension scheme. the pension fund has now run into payment difficulties and a deficit has been created. the fdp in the european parliament is opposed to the compensation of the deficit from taxation. it is irresponsible to make the european taxpayer pay for these losses. such plans must be prevented. the fdp in the european parliament votes against the discharge of the european parliament's budget. the possibility of offsetting the deficit with taxpayers' money is not completely excluded.
in writing. - the report of the committee on transport does not take sufficient account of the real interests of rail transport as a whole in the better use of existing capacity. infrastructure managers should be required to reserve capacity for occasional services in the annual network timetable. this ex ante obligation does not give the infrastructure managers any flexibility to decide on such a measure in a timely manner. the commission's original proposal was even tightened up, as the reserve capacity must guarantee sufficient quality for international facilitated freight routes. the volume of short-term track applications by railway undertakings actually used cannot be estimated from a planning perspective. these capacities are removed from the timetable-making process in advance, with the consequence that subsequent other route requests cannot be met. if the already scarce network capacity is not used by the freight transport companies, it is finally destroyed to the detriment of all users. this would achieve the exact opposite of the actual objective of better use of existing capacity. in order to limit the negative impact on passenger traffic and on short-term freight traffic, it is necessary to provide for rules which leave it to the infrastructure managers to decide whether such a measure is appropriate, taking into account the interests of rail passenger transport, or how the needs of rail freight transport can be better addressed.
in writing. - i voted for the directive on patients' rights in crossborder healthcare, as it brings more legal certainty for patients. particularly for the border areas of the european union, such as my home in the greater germany region, belgium, luxembourg, france or for rural regions with a medical shortage, the promotion of patient mobility is an important building block for improving and increasing efficiency in health care. the german healthcare sector will benefit from cross-border patient mobility as patients from other eu countries make greater use of our high-quality medical services, for example in rehabilitation. the member states' sovereignty must be maintained. the member states are responsible for the provision of medical care and the organisation of their health systems. in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, the directive is intended to cover only those areas which concern the cross-border mobility of patients. our high quality and safety standards in germany must be maintained. ethical standards that member states adhere to for good reasons, such as in artificial insemination, dna analysis or assisted suicide, must not be called into question.
in writing. - the explicit demand in amendment no 15 for the eradication of rare hereditary diseases by genetic counselling of parents who are carriers of the disease and the selection of healthy embryos by pre-implantation diagnosis (pid) is not only contrary to the law in force in germany. in the particular context of german history, it seems in principle to be intolerable and intolerable to demand or recommend the elimination and selection of potentially disabled people, even if they are not yet born. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the proposed supplementary proposal replaces the promotion of the therapeutic treatment of rare diseases with the aim of preventing the birth of sick people. this is not in keeping with the spirit and content of european and international human rights declarations. the real aim of a convincing european policy should be to help people who are affected or threatened by disease, rather than selecting them early on on the basis of quality criteria. the report and the individual amendments, in particular amendment no 15, do not reflect my fundamental christian values. that is why i voted against the report.

the tragic images from the media of thousands of volunteers on the coast of the affected areas, deployed to clean up the damage, watching helplessly as birds and other fauna and flora die in the black flood. it was clear that everything possible had to be done to prevent similar catastrophes from happening again. it was clear that we had to work together. it was clear that the european union had to send a signal that ships in distress, without insurance, not complying with the basic safety rules, had no place on european shores. in response, in november 2005 the european commission presented a set of eight ambitious legislative proposals, the so-called third maritime safety package. the package will bring tangible results for europe in the form of better prevention of maritime accidents, more frequent inspections and a clear division of responsibilities towards ship operators. the results of this european legislation, apart from the incalculable impact on the environment, which is the capital of us all, will be appreciated not only by citizens and businesses in the maritime states, as it might seem, but also by export-oriented landlocked states such as my country, where a large part of production is shipped out of europe by sea. inland, too, there is a vital interest in ensuring that no more erika or prestige tankers are sailing off european coasts and that maritime transport is carried out efficiently, safely and in an environmentally sound manner. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me conclude by taking this opportunity to thank the rapporteurs of the discussions in the council for four long years before the council finally reached its common position on its content in june last year, after very complicated negotiations. a qualified majority of member states agreed that the key point of contention, the so-called opt-out, would be retained in the directive for the future, but with firmly defined conditions that would make its application very restrictive. for example, the council wanted the maximum limit on the length of weekly working hours for opt-outs to be reduced from 78 hours to 60 or 65 hours, it proposed a ban on negotiating opt-outs when signing employment contracts, or limiting the period of consent given by employees to work in opt-out mode to one year. the council's aim was to limit the use of opt-outs in the member states, but above all to increase the protection of the employee who would opt-out. the council considered its draft directive to be balanced, enhancing the protection of workers, and hoped that it would be acceptable to parliament and that parliament would adopt it at second reading. the czech presidency was fully aware of the differences in the positions of the two institutions on the draft directive after the vote last december, but at the same time it did not see the conciliation procedure as a battle of prestige between the institutions, but instead advocated a pragmatic, non-ideological and realistic approach that would take into account the reality of the european labour market. it is an indisputable fact that opt-outs are now used in 15 of the 27 eu member states. since the czech republic took over the presidency of the council in january this year, we have been engaged in very intensive negotiations at all levels with the aim of finding a real space for a possible compromise with parliament. the first meeting of the member states on this subject took place in prague on 13 january. there have been at least eight rounds of informal trialogue and, very unusually, three rounds of the conciliation procedure itself. at this point, let me thank the commission, and in particular commissioner spidlov, for his expertise and constructive approach in seeking a possible compromise on the text of the directive. the council was willing to compromise, to discount the common position, and yet in the end, no agreement was reached. during the last four months, the czech presidency has been very active and responsible in its negotiations with parliament, presenting a series of compromise proposals on the various aspects of the directive, with a view to reaching a final solution that would be acceptable to both the council and parliament. today i can say with some responsibility that the council has made a number of significant concessions to parliament's demands, and yet this has not been enough for parliament. for example, the council was willing to abandon the common position and accept the view of the parliament that all standby working time is working time. the council also made concessions in the discussion on reconciliation of work and family life, the time limit for granting alternative daily rest and the definition of senior staff, and i could go on. the council also wanted to reach agreement with parliament on the key issue of opt-outs and was willing to go along with parliament and accepted its other proposals, such as the prohibition of opt-outs during probationary periods, the removal of the maximum weekly working time limit for opt-outs, although we naturally felt that we were acting against the interests of employees, and we were also willing to accept the introduction of a record of the time actually worked in opt-outs. parliament did not, however, meet the council. on behalf of the czech presidency, i sincerely regret that parliament was unwilling to accept a compromise and agree to a revision of the directive, which not only the member states but also the citizens of the european union have been waiting for for five years. the adoption of a revision of the directive would contribute to greater protection of workers, to addressing issues of work alertness and rest, and to creating the conditions for a gradual reduction in the use of opt-outs in the member states. but your representatives on the negotiating committee have not heard those arguments. they refused to accept them, they refused to accept the council's favourable proposals and the commission's compromises, and they maintained their ideological position. since parliament was unwilling to respect the situation in the council and the current reality, the existing directive will continue to apply. there will continue to be no restrictions on the use of opt-outs or monitoring, and workers will be able to continue working up to 78 hours a week. parliament's position is likely to result in further expansion of the use of opt-outs. the european commission already has indications from two other countries that they will decide to introduce it, and therefore the hope of its future abolition is even lower. the council wanted to prevent this, but parliament decided otherwise.
member of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i am very sorry that the council and parliament have not been able to reach agreement in the final round of negotiations on the revision of the working time directive. the commission did all it could to reach a compromise, putting forward a series of proposals covering all the main issues to help the two legislators get closer to the final version. however, the council and parliament ultimately insisted on their differing views on the future of the opt-outs, which could not be reconciled. i understand and respect parliament's wish to put an end to the use of exceptions once and for all. that would be ideal for me too, and we also included this element in the commission's proposal to amend the directive in 2005. however, after several years of negotiations, it has become clear that this will not ensure agreement in the council, that it will not overcome the blocking minority. too many member states simply insisted that individual exemptions should be possible and that this possibility should be maintained in the directive. the commission therefore put forward alternative proposals aimed at improving the legal protection of workers benefiting from derogations and de facto weakening their use, introducing close monitoring of the use of derogations at national and european level and establishing limits to the current use of derogations, thus also making the granting of derogations increasingly unattractive to member states. we believe that this approach would actually improve the conditions of workers in practice and, more importantly, increase the long-term prospects for member states to move towards abolishing exemptions. parliament took the view that there was no better arrangement than one which explicitly provided for the abolition of the opt-out. i respect the reasons for this decision, but i take a different view. as i have said many times before, i am fully convinced that the failure to reach agreement on the amendment is bad news for european workers and businesses, for european institutions and, ultimately, for europe as a whole. firstly, it does not address the issue of exceptions which will continue to be used in accordance with the current directive without a date for their expiry and with a very small number of restrictions and without any specific review. i know that many of you have objected to workers working 65 hours a week, and i understand those concerns, but the fact is that the current directive allows for up to 70 hours a week. secondly, although the court of justice's decisions on standby time and compensatory rest periods will remain unchanged, i am afraid that in practice this will not lead to better protection of workers in many cases. in a number of member states, high-precision industries have real difficulties in complying with the rules stemming from the simap, jaeger judgments. the result so far is that even more member states have started to use exceptions to solve this problem. there are currently 15 of them, and i am concerned that now that there is no agreement on the standby time, even more member states will start to use opt-outs to comply with the european court of justice's decision, because they will have no other choice. with the growing number of states benefiting from the derogation, it will be much more difficult to reach agreement in the council on its termination. thirdly, the failure of the negotiations means that a number of very important specific guarantees approved by the council for workers throughout europe who are already benefiting from the derogations will not apply, will not come into force. finally, we will also prepare for the possibility of improvements in the measures to ensure a balance between work and family life and a clearer definition of the derogation for the self-employed. however, both legislators have already taken a decision and the immediate consequence will be the failure to carry out the special review of exceptions required by the current working time directive. i respect that decision. we will now have to reflect with the other members of the commission on the situation that has arisen as a result of the disagreement between the legislators. i would like to say, however, that after five years of negotiations, during which a number of sub-proposals were put forward, during which a number of attempts were made to find a way forward, we have not found that way. this means that it is not easy to come up with a new proposal that will solve the situation by miracle. i therefore consider it necessary to consult the social partners very carefully on the situation and only then will the commission be able to take any further decisions and proceedings.

president-in-office of the council. − madam president, we are all aware that we are continuing to suffer from one of the most severe financial and economic crises for many years. the union and the member states have taken a wide range of measures both to try to mitigate the effects of this crisis, and also to address some of its root causes, while also taking into account the pressing need to better prepare ourselves for the future in order to face the challenges of the global economy. we are also aware that the current difficulties are not simply about figures on balance sheets, or amending economic forecasts. they have a real impact on people: on their livelihoods, on their families, and on their standards of living. most directly affected are those who have already lost their jobs as a result, or the many more who risk losing their jobs over the months to come. the spring european council agreed that an employment summit should be held in order to allow for an exchange of experiences on the extent to which the recovery measures taken have succeeded in supporting employment and creating new jobs and more jobs. the summit will take place in prague this thursday. the mandate given to the presidency was clear. we need to examine issues such as maintaining employment levels through flexicurity and mobility, creating a favourable environment for investments and job creation by businesses, especially small and medium-sized ones, upgrading skills and anticipating labour market needs. we must also look at strengthening and restructuring the labour market so as to prepare it for the future. our objective is to ensure that the summit is not just an opportunity to talk, but that it produces concrete outcomes and recommendations which will benefit society as a whole. the participants will include the social troika at the level of the prime ministers and employment ministers of the current czech presidency and of the forthcoming swedish and spanish presidencies. the social partners will be represented by the presidents and general secretaries of business europe and the european trade union confederation, together with the representatives of small and medium-sized undertakings and public-sector employers. the european commission will be represented by president barroso and commissioner špidla. the chairs of the employment committee, the social protection committee and the economic policy committee will also be present. representatives of the european parliament have, of course, been invited as well. it is also my understanding that the president of the european parliament, mr pöttering, is going to attend. in order to help prepare for the summit, three workshops have been organised in the countries of the three participating delegations: in madrid, in stockholm and in prague. these workshops have especially addressed the issues of upgrading skills, increasing access to employment, and how to maintain employment, create jobs and promote mobility. these workshops have enabled us to focus, with the social partners, on the key areas of concern. we were pleased that the representative of the european parliament attended the preparatory workshops – namely mr andersson, chair of the committee on employment and social affairs. the workshop on skills upgrading, which took place in madrid, highlighted that skills are the key to preparing for the future. in the short term, skills increase both productivity and mobility. in the longer term, they pave the way to recovery, increase competitiveness and are crucial for reducing exclusion and promoting greater social equality. the case for upgrading skills, which is endorsed by all stakeholders, is not just about formal qualifications, but also about promoting areas such as communication skills amongst young people. the issue of financing the acquisition of higher skills cannot be overlooked, especially in a time of crisis. it requires commitment not only from the public authorities, but also from employers and from workers and job-seekers themselves. at eu level, there is a need to explore further the possibilities of using the european social fund. as far as employers are concerned, their own interest in developing skills is self-evident, as firms which fail to invest in skills upgrading are two and a half times more likely to go out of business than those that do. the workshop in stockholm on increasing access to employment focused on how to get the newly unemployed and the inactive into – or back into – jobs as quickly as possible. the newly-unemployed should not be allowed to become long-term unemployed. it is particularly important to ensure that social protection systems serve as a springboard into new jobs, and not just as passive safety nets. a need for incentives to actively seek employment cannot be overlooked. a flexicurity approach should contribute to making transitions pay, not least by providing the necessary element of security. during this workshop in stockholm, it was also stressed that the short-term measures should not be allowed to prejudice the longer term. early retirement schemes are a poor solution to providing more jobs for the young, as they lower overall participation rates, and are inevitably accompanied by higher social security costs. at eu level, the possible use of the european social fund for funding active inclusion measures was identified, as was the possibility of enabling older workers to stay in employment by reducing their social security contributions. at the last workshop, which took place in prague last week, the need to maintain employment and to improve an environment friendly to entrepreneurship and job creation was emphasised. the temporary short-term working arrangements can be beneficial, but their financial sustainability needs to be ensured. however, we must guard against the trend to protectionism, which can only harm the union as a whole. we also need to use active measures to promote mobility and again, in this context, the increased flexibility of our labour markets has a key role to play. despite the impact of the crisis, there are still a substantial number of vacancies in europe, but there is a lack of coordination both within and between the member states. often, people are in the wrong place, or lack the right skills, or a combination of both. it is clear from these workshops that the present crisis is not just cyclical, but structural. profound changes are going to be needed to face stiff competition in a globalised economy and to safeguard long-term employment in the eu. however, in many instances, these changes are actually about continuing initiatives or even accelerating the overdue reforms which have been pursued for many years in the context of the european employment strategy. apart from the efforts to maintain current jobs, we must also create a favourable environment for investors and businesses to invest and create new jobs. we cannot keep all existing jobs: the crisis requires structural change and people will lose jobs. but we must offer the unemployed a chance to improve their skills and employability, and to quickly find a new job which has been created somewhere else. let me also briefly touch upon some other topics which you will discuss here today during your social agenda debate. i congratulate mr silva peneda, in particular, on his extensive and far-reaching report which covers a wide range of issues, and which calls specifically for an ambitious social policy agenda. mr peneda’s report underlines the need for job creation and flexibility in the workplace as part of europe’s broader social policy. it also recognises the importance of developing new skills, of lifelong learning and of promoting university-business cooperation. these are all key aspects which will also be taken up as part of our agenda for this week’s summit. this wide-ranging report is complemented by that of ms lambert on how to include people who are frequently excluded from the labour market. this week’s summit will certainly need to take into account this important goal. we cannot and will not seek to push job creation for a few. our objective – even more so in the current difficult climate – is to adopt an inclusive approach to employment policy. the czech presidency supports the long-term employment targets of the european union and has repeatedly emphasised the need to better motivate people to seek employment and to improve their employability. we all probably agree that it is better if people earn their living themselves and are free instead of being dependent on the social protection system. this is why we need to reduce the segmentation of our labour markets. the global adjustment fund provides support for workers made redundant as a result of globalisation. i am pleased that there is agreement between parliament and the council on amending the fund, and i am grateful to ms stauner for her work on this. by introducing greater flexibility in how the fund is used and by reducing the number of redundancies from 1 000 to 500, it will become an ever more effective instrument for helping to tackle the effects of the economic down-turn. let me conclude by saying that the most urgent need now is to ensure that the many ideas which have emerged from preparatory workshops, and which will shape the debate at this week’s employment summit, are translated into action. as i said at the outset, we are looking for a concrete outcome which will benefit society as a whole, as well as european citizens. we cannot hope to resolve the effects of the current crisis in a single meeting, but we should focus on specific recommendations and initiatives which will together play a role in mitigating the effects of the crisis and help us emerge from it even stronger.
president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the sharp rise in unemployment is the most dramatic consequence of the world economic crisis. it affects individuals and families, and it brings real hardship. it affects society, it robs it of its vitality, it affects the economy, which loses skills and experience that will take years to rebuild. this is where the human cost of the crisis is felt most strongly. unemployment is a local, national and european phenomenon. within the european market, where more and more citizens are exercising their right to free movement, employment has long been a matter of national and european policy. it is therefore essential to design the responses from a european perspective. unemployment is our first concern in the commission. the commission is working tirelessly to ensure that all those with political responsibilities in europe hear this call and devote all their energies to finding a way out of the crisis. i know that in the european parliament i do not need to explain the weight and the seriousness of unemployment. every day one of your constituents loses his job, three others fear the same fate. in march, the european council endorsed the initiative of the commission and the czech presidency of the council to devise a summit on the employment aspect of the economic and financial crisis. this has been a central concern of ours since the beginning of the crisis and it inspired our proposal for a european economic recovery plan last december. its implementation at national and european level is already playing a major role in preserving jobs and creating new ones. but it is urgent to assess its impact on employment. we must learn from them and adapt our actions in the months ahead. i still think format. in any case, this is no reason for the commission to lower its ambitions as regards the content of this employment summit and its follow-up during the forthcoming swedish and spanish presidencies. the european dimension is essential for two main reasons. firstly, we must send a clear signal to the citizens that the european union understands the true nature of the crisis, that it technical measures to solve regulatory problems. it must be based on our fundamental values: solidarity, social justice, and so on. and our response must be seen as such, as a response that flows from member of the commission. − mr president, the current economic downturn requires a stimulus also at eu level. this has been our common conviction since the crisis began last year. in november 2008 the european commission proposed a comprehensive european economic recovery plan, which was endorsed by heads of state and government in december. building on this, a ‘five billion package’ to inject immediate stimulus into the eu economy was proposed in january. the package directs that stimulus to key objectives, such as broadband development, energy security and low-carbon technologies. the commission very much welcomes the agreement found on the package, after difficult but constructive discussions, within a very tight timeframe. i would like to thank parliament for its support for our proposal, as well as its flexibility and sense of compromise shown in the course of interinstitutional discussions. this case shows that the eu is able to react quickly if a crisis requires an immediate response. as regards the budget side – and now i am speaking on behalf of vice-president kallas – the commission can accept the solution as now agreed by the three institutions, though its approach differs from our initial proposal of december 2008. we are confident that the projects will be implemented as scheduled. i would also like to confirm that the commission has taken good note of parliament’s expectations with regard to the budget review and the assessment of the functioning of the interinstitutional agreement. as you know, we are working on these issues and will come forward with our conclusions in the autumn or, at the latest, by the end of the year. i will now turn to my subject: energy. the regulation on energy projects constitutes a significant tool to achieve two goals: responding to the key security issues and environmental challenges in the energy sector whilst at the same time contributing to the recovery of our economy. the package is also an example of solidarity within the european union. in particular, the gas crises needed a quick response. never before has the european union agreed to dedicate such a significant amount to key energy projects. i know that some of you would have preferred to see more measures on renewables and energy efficiency projects in the package, but i believe that the compromise finally found on this subject is a good one. the commission provides reassurance in a comprehensive declaration that it will reconsider the situation in 2010, referring expressly to the option of suggesting using uncommitted funds for measures in the area of energy efficiency and renewable energy sources. the declaration was sent to parliament and will be published in the official journal, together with the regulation, so i will not read it out here. i welcome the fact that the principle of proposing new projects, if we identify serious risks in implementing the current projects, is also referred to in the recitals and an article of the regulation. in addition, i can assure you that we will swiftly go ahead with the many other initiatives in the area of renewable energy sources and energy efficiency, as they are referred to in our declaration. after the successful and rapid conclusion of the legislative procedure, the commission will focus on implementation of the package. i can tell you that, with respect to the energy projects, we intend to launch the call for proposals by the end of may, and i expect first decisions on support by the end of this year. i would like to thank particularly the rapporteurs, ms stavreva, mr maldeikis and mr böge, for their engagement in finding a quick solution to this very important proposal.
