mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the financial crisis has made it clear that the financial market framework of the european union needs to be redesigned. my group supports the proposals developed in the trilogue negotiations, in particular the proposal for a new own funds directive for banks. risk-taking will increase, the misuse of special purpose vehicles will disappear and the quality of structured products will improve because of the 5% deduction for securitisations. however, i regret that the rules on interbank loans below maturity are very restrictive and that silent partnership contributions are only accepted as full-value equity for a transitional period. progress in the restructuring of the financial market framework is good, but it is not yet sufficient. so the work will continue. i hope that in future the banks will be more cooperative in this work than in the past few months, when i have seen them more in the role of a brake than a partner looking for forward-looking solutions.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i should like to say first of all that with this second project we are discussing today we have started to put financial market regulation on a normal footing. the financial crisis is partly due to market failure and partly to regulatory failure. we have a list of measures that absolutely need to be regulated by the rating agencies. we have taken decisions on the equity directive, on manager's remuneration, on hedge funds, on accounting rules and on the european supervisory structure. we are at the second point today. it was negotiated here on the basis of a committee vote, not the normal first reading procedure, but by agreement between the council, the commission and parliament before parliament's first reading. mr karas has done a great deal of work here, and i should like to expressly acknowledge that. but i have a number of colleagues who disagree with me on two points. and this concerns first of all the risk reserve. the securitisation market and the financial market crisis were created in part because financial market products were created without any risk of their own. that is why banks no longer trust each other, because no one has securities for which he is willing to take risks. here, five percent is suggested. i think that 10% is much more appropriate and that is why i have tabled an amendment to that effect. i am sure that if the council accepts all the other things, it will also have to consider this 10 per cent. we as a parliament have a responsibility to give citizens additional assurances that such a global financial market crisis cannot happen again. i therefore propose and ask that we accept the compromise worked out by mr karas, with the exception of the 10% reserve and the continued credit of silent partnership contributions.

securitisation and pointed out the good aspects of it and the amount of money that is contributed to the capital markets for small and medium-sized enterprises and to lenders at large in all member states of the european union. in case there is any impression that i do not see the benefits of securitisation over the years, may i say that i certainly do! in my previous capacity, and long before i came here, i was aware of the benefits of securitisations. however, the issue is what proportion the originating securitiser should hold in that particular matter. i accept what mrs bowles said: that in future a holding of whatever percentage will attract a capital charge. one cannot be certain as to when the current financial crisis will end. but, irrespective of when that end is going to be, i think we can be absolutely certain in years to come that financial institutions will be required, at all levels, to hold more significant and more quality capital against their lending. i will not be here – but many of you will – but, whatever the end is, that will be the inevitable outcome of this particular financial crisis – not immediately, not maybe in the medium term, but in the longer term that will be a certainty. if i looked into my crystal ball, that is what i would see in years to come. so it is the percentage which is being debated. people know my views on this. i have held very strong views on this for a long period of time. various amendments have been put forward during the council of ministers stage and with the european parliament about different ‘outs’ on one thing and another, which my officials, at my request, are very, very strongly against, because i strongly believe in the very simple proposition that 5% of something is better than 55% of zero. the more outs that there are – we can have 5%, 10%, 15% – 15% of zero is still zero. that is why i welcome the opportunity that the commission in its report by the end of this year will come back to this particular matter in order to ensure that the wording is fairly tightened up. i am strongly of that view because i do not wish to see particular outs. but i readily appreciate what mrs bowles and others have said regarding the merits of securitisations for the capital market. i hope i have never given the impression that i did not. finally, may i, too, join with the president in wishing those members who considered and not dogmatic, and i wish him, in particular, a very successful future.

in writing. the spd meps did not agree with karas' report for two reasons: firstly, the credit securitisation reserve is an important and correct instrument for financial institutions to share in the business risk. however, this requires a significant amount of own resources. the 5% deduction agreed in the trilogue does not meet this condition. the eu commission had originally asked for 15 per cent in the consultation process, but then bowed to industry pressure and proposed 5 per cent. the conservatives and liberals in the economic and monetary committee wanted to declare even this small share of the business risk superfluous when a guarantee declaration was presented by the financial institutions. the spd meps are in favour of a significantly higher deductible and will continue to press this demand in future reforms of the equity capital directives. secondly, the definition of core capital as given in the karas report violates the competition neutrality of the scheme. it provides that in future silent partnership contributions will no longer be fully considered core capital, although they may be fully absorbed in the event of liquidity. this opens the door to unfair competition from public banks in germany. we find that silent partnership contributions are a proven and eu-compliant refinancing instrument. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
in the present financial crisis, the european social models are facing major challenges. the cdu/csu group therefore advocates a social europe. we are therefore behind the report by josé silva peneda on the renewed social agenda. we therefore welcome the fact that priority is being given to creating and promoting jobs in these times of crisis and that we want to promote educational policy measures. europe must create a social framework and set standards at the european level. however, the following areas of competence of the member states must be respected: we have therefore opposed the papal call for the introduction of minimum wages in all the member states, which was originally called for in paragraph 14 of the report. the introduction of minimum wages is a purely national decision. we therefore welcome the success of the oral amendment on this point. every person must be guaranteed adequate resources to live a life in dignity, but member states have different options to ensure this. we have made it clear in our oral amendment that, in addition to minimum wages, collective agreements and generally binding regulations or a state guaranteed minimum income are also considered. in this way we are taking account of the principle of subsidiarity.

president-in-office of the council. − last march the council and the spring european council further refined a new position for the international climate change negotiations, in particular in view of the copenhagen conference. at this meeting of 19-20 march 2009, the council stressed its conviction that the economic crisis and the policy measures in response to it provide an opportunity to achieve the necessary economic reforms and at the same time speed up reforms towards a safe and sustainable low-carbon resource-efficient economy. the presidency conclusions of the european council of march this year stated that the european union remained committed to playing a leading role and bringing about the global and comprehensive climate agreement in copenhagen in december this year, designed to limit global warming to below 2° celsius. to this end the european council recalled the eu’s commitment to a 30% emission reduction as its contribution to such an agreement, provided that other developed countries commit themselves to comparable emission reductions and that advanced developing countries contribute adequately according to their responsibilities and respective capabilities. the european council will further discuss these issues at its june meeting.

regional cooperation and good neighbourly relations among the western balkan countries. regional cooperation and the european agenda are linked. the more western balkan countries cooperate with each other, the more they integrate within european structures. this is because regional cooperation contributes to a shared understanding in the region and to finding solutions for issues of common interest, such as in the fields of energy, transport, trade, the fight against organised crime and corruption, refugee return and border control.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. this is my last speech to the european parliament and i am pleased to be speaking as accept all of this. before i leave office, i would like to thank all the colleagues from the epp-ed group, the spe group, the liberal group and the green group who supported me in my report. i would like to thank jo leinen, chairman of the constitutional committee, and in particular all the coordinators and shadow rapporteurs of these four groups. i thank you for the excellent cooperation we have had across party and national boundaries and for the way we have been able to advance the european integration project together. the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the provision on the citizens' initiative in the lisbon treaty is undoubtedly a milestone in the process of european integration. because it is true: in the european union we are not uniting states, we are uniting people. this concern will be met in a new quality when citizens themselves are directly involved in the european legislative process for the first time, as provided for in article 11 (4) of the new eu treaty. a million citizens will then have the same right to ask the commission to submit a specific draft regulation or directive as the council has had since 1957 and the european parliament since 1993. in my report, parliament sets out the main points and guidelines for a future regulation on the conditions and procedures for a european citizens' initiative. and, madam vice-president, i expect the commission, in the event of the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, not only to submit a proposal as soon as possible, but also to follow the guidelines of my report as far as possible. in particular, the commission should share the view of parliament, which represents a significant number of member states within the meaning of article 11 (4) of the new eu treaty. my report proposes the number 7. it is of key importance that no arbitrary number is fixed here, because it must be able to justify the related restriction on the right of citizens of the union to participate on an equal footing in a citizens' initiative, irrespective of their nationality, on the one hand, and be purpose-oriented on the other. in other words, the minimum number of member states must ensure that the starting point of the european legislative process is sufficiently determined by the general european interest and not by national particular interests. i would also like to ask you to pay particular attention to the design of the procedure, in particular to the question of the admissibility of a citizens' initiative. the european parliament has already adopted a resolution on the situation in the former yugoslavia. if citizens of the union want to have a say in the european legislative process and launch a citizens' initiative, it is essentially a matter of fairness that the competent union institutions give their opinion as early as possible and, above all, in a binding manner on whether the proposed initiative fulfils the legal requirements of the treaty. this should be done before the collection of statements of support, because the member states that provide resources for this need legal certainty too. in conclusion, i would like to remind you that the provisions on the citizens' initiative did not fall from the sky. they were already in the constitutional treaty, because they were developed in the constitutional convention - some of my colleagues were involved in this - in close cooperation with non-governmental organisations. its inclusion in the convention's draft constitution was neither spontaneous nor a product of chance. it was rather the result of intensive consultations between members of the convention and non-governmental organisations committed to democratic politics. and by now -- you know this -- this idea has been on hold for six years. i think it is high time that this idea was finally brought to life after so long, because it is high time for direct democracy in a united europe! between european film industry professionals and those from all over the world. the concept of media mundus is new, ambitious and innovative, because it promotes cooperation between professionals, which is not done normally by european programmes, and, unlike existing programmes, it is also based on mutual benefit, not only for our film-makers but also for film-makers from third countries, in vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, once again, as a former colleague, i would like to thank the committee on transport and its chairman for the fruitful work they have done when i was a member of parliament and for the cooperation they have given me since i had the honour of being supported, by the vote of parliament, as european commissioner for transport. and this fruitful cooperation, ladies and gentlemen, is also being seen today, because i cannot, on this occasion too, fail to thank parliament, and in particular the committee on transport, chaired by mr costa, for the speed with which they have dealt with the european commission's proposal on the time bands. a number of events - the economic and financial crisis, the new influenza a virus - are further aggravating the situation in the air transport sector, and this situation shows how urgent and indispensable support measures are, not only for airlines but also for airline employees. that said, i share president costa's concern. the commission proposal is not a definitive and final proposal. perhaps it is a proposal to deal with an emergency, but it needs a thorough review to redesign the whole system, so much so that on 15 april, in response to the concerns and comments of president costa, i announced to him, as chairman of the committee, that the services of the european commission's directorate-general for transport and energy are already working to submit a proposal for a rapid revision of the regulation. the suspension of the rule on the use of time bands has already been used twice in the past to deal with the crisis. it is a global response to a global crisis, a response that obviously does not concern one or two member states, it concerns the air transport system of the whole european union and, in the moments of the most serious crisis - the attacks of september 11 and the sars crisis, severe acute respiratory syndrome - similar measures were taken. and the crisis affecting the air transport sector today is probably more serious than any previous one and we have no idea yet when we will start to see improvements. the reality is that traffic is falling all the time. the suspension of the "use it or lose it" rule for the summer season will benefit all airlines, european and non-european, without any discrimination, as iata and many non-european airlines have also stressed. i am sure that this measure, which will be limited in time and will be of an isolated nature - the suspension will be in effect for the period between 29 march and 26 october this year and will then allow slots to be kept in the summer season of next year - will give all the airlines a breathing space, allowing them to cope with the fall in demand. it will also avoid paradoxical situations such as the present one, where companies are forced to fly empty in order not to lose slots, which i also find absolutely unacceptable from an environmental point of view, as well as being harmful to the economies of companies. we know that when a company is in difficulty, the workers who are part of that company are also in difficulty. i am sure that this measure is necessary and urgent, and i can therefore only support the compromise reached between parliament and the council, which will allow the proposal to be adopted immediately. i would like to thank the chairman of the committee on transport and the whole house once again for this.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. mr president, mr vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the epp-ed group supports the one-off suspension of the 80% minimum utilisation rule for airlines' rights to take-off and land at airports for the 2010 summer timetable proposed by the commission and thanks rapporteur paolo costa for his swift and effective handling of this dossier. this suspension now allows airlines to cancel flights beyond the minimum planned use in response to declining demand without losing their take-off and landing rights for the next season. i think this is uniquely justified, as the vice-president has said, because there have been unforeseeable declines in passenger numbers as a result of the international financial and economic crisis and because there is no way for airlines to predict how passenger numbers will develop in the future. this suspension is also to protect the environment, as airlines might otherwise feel compelled to operate low-load flights just to keep the slots. but, mr commissioner, mr vice-president, the epp-ed group has rejected from the outset the scheme you have also proposed, which would have empowered the commission to extend the suspension of the rule without any real involvement of parliament, simply by means of the comitology procedure. we believe that if you were to make such a proposal for the winter timetable, parliament would have to consider it carefully, because we would then have to examine more carefully the interests of the airlines - on the industrial and social aspects, and my colleague, neelie kroes, will be speaking on the aid aspects. 12 million workers are directly or indirectly employed by european car manufacturers. this is why the commission met with all stakeholders, including member states and social partners, in october 2008 as part of the cars-21 process to discuss a common approach to crisis management. the meeting discussed scrappage premiums and additional eib financing to prevent this sector, which is important for employment, from being swallowed up by the crisis. we must also act to ensure that our legal commitments to reduce co2 emissions from cars by 2012 are not jeopardised by the crisis. i'll get back to you on that. the commission, concerned about the developments around general motors, had already called a political meeting of all member states in january this year to create transparency to ensure compliance with european rules. three such meetings have taken place so far. these meetings have been the occasion for the adoption and publication of joint political agreements within the 27 member states. first, it was agreed that the german-coordinated trust arrangement was the right way to protect general motors europe from the insolvency of its american parent. we can now say that this trust arrangement has prevented the european car manufacturers from being dragged into the bankruptcy of general motors. secondly, it was agreed that the trust arrangement does not constitute a prior decision in favour of a bidder. as regards the selection of a bidder, the commission has stated from the outset that it will be neutral, otherwise the commission cannot fulfil its role as guardian of the contracts. it was also agreed that all national safeguard measures must be fully compatible with the state aid and internal market provisions of the ec treaty. state aid must therefore not be made conditional on political conditions such as the location of the investments. the eu treaty has no place for economic nationalism. public funds may only be used exceptionally and only where sustainable economic structures with sustainable jobs are created. all decisions must be based member of the commission. − mr president, a large potential for new exporting opportunities lies in the asian markets that have high growth rates but also, of course, high barriers to entry. apart from the multilateral talks, an important way to overcome these barriers is through the leverage available to us in free trade agreement negotiations. that is why member states have asked the commission to launch a new generation of trade agreements with key asian economies. these free trade agreements should be ambitious in creating new exporting opportunities for many sectors. with korea this is what we have achieved after two intensive years of negotiations. this is the most ambitious free trade agreement ever negotiated by the european union. there is consensus that in two of the three main sectors of our economy the benefits from the free trade agreement are overwhelmingly in our favour: first of all, our competitive service providers will gain massively from the agreement. for example, in areas such as telecoms, transport, construction and environmental services, doing business in korea will be much easier in the future. secondly, for agricultural products, korea will eliminate almost all of its particularly high tariffs – they average 35%! that will give a boost to farming exports of, amongst other things, pork, wine, whisky or dairy products. we will also secure the protection of european geographical indications, such as parma ham, rioja or tokay. but the free trade agreement will also bring major benefits to european manufacturing exporters. overall, european manufacturing exporters will save some eur 1.2 billion of tariffs annually, of which eur 800 million are saved on day one. for example, exporters of machineries would save eur 450 million annually on annual duty payments. exporters of chemicals would save over eur 150 million on duties. duty elimination will also allow our exporters to strengthen their foothold in the korean market, and thus expand sales. korean customers buy some eur 25 billion worth of eu goods every year. this makes korea one of our most important export markets in asia. in addition, there was a special focus on rules. the agreement includes transparency on regulation, efficient enforcement of commitments, better protection of intellectual property rights and ‘wto-plus’ rules on subsidies which will all be to the benefit of all manufacturers selling in korea. moreover, ambitious disciplines have been established on industrial technical barriers to trade, notably for cars, electronics and pharmaceuticals based on the regulatory model of europe and they respond to longstanding demands by european business in these sectors. korea will need to changes its domestic regulations to comply with these commitments, whereas no such change would be needed in europe. concerning the car industry specifically, i want to signal first of all that we also have an interest in enhancing market access for european cars in korea. our car exporters are by far the strongest importers on the korean market, with strong growth rates. they can develop this further since they will benefit from the combination of elimination of tariffs – eur 2 000 saved on a car worth eur 25 000 – and the removal of technical obstacles. the agreement negotiated includes the most ambitious disciplines for non-tariff barriers ever negotiated with a third country. korea will accept from day one that a car that conforms to international standards will be considered as complying with those korean regulations that have been signalled by our industry as representing significant obstacles. there are also provisions by which korea accepts the equivalence between european and korean environmental regulations. indeed, even before the agreement enters into force, korea has agreed to apply certain transitional derogations from the korean environmental standards important for our exporters and we are monitoring very closely discussions in korea about new regulations to limit co2 emissions in order to make them show that they are not an impediment to trade. we are aware of the sensitivities of the car sector. we defended long transition periods for the liberalisation of our most sensitive car segment, namely small cars. tariffs will only be eliminated in year five of the agreement, and that allows time for adjustment. we should remember the significant korean investment in the car sector in europe. moderately, we have changed the rules of origin by increasing the permissible limit of foreign value in korean cars from 40% to 45%, and we agreed a bilateral safeguard clause which lets us put up tariffs in case of a surge of imports and a threat of injury to our industries. on duty drawback, my final point, this is nothing new. such policies are legitimate under the world trade organisation. duty drawback also does not create a significant competitive disadvantage for our car producers since our tariffs on car parts are generally very low and will be further reduced. and we have we negotiated a special clause that would enable us to limit duty drawback efficiently. i underline the strength of support from european manufacturing sectors, as well as agriculture and service organisations for this agreement. this is important, and it is a clear signal of our determination to pursue market access interest in key emerging asian economies.

member of the commission. − we work actively to tackle what are very complex vital sanitary barriers, and with this to help market the sale of european products like irish beef and lamb. the market access strategy, and particularly the market access partnership launched in 2007, is the centrepiece of the commission’s work in that respect. the market access strategy sets up a stronger partnership between commission, member states and business to enhance the work of detecting, analysing, prioritising and removing barriers. the specificity of this strategy is that it is done through the right mix of various trade policy instruments. that means using multilateral and bilateral channels and complementing the more formal medium to long-term policy instruments with political contacts and with joint trade diplomacy. our efforts in relation to this market access have been stepped up considerably in recent years, and we have several success stories to show we are going in the right direction. for example, we managed to confine a few countries and lift the ban on eu exports of meat due to the dioxin and pcbs contamination incident in ireland in december 2008, and recently we were successful in opening saudi arabia, jordan and the philippines to the input of eu beef and to treat certain sps issues in a more trade-friendly manner with egypt and israel. we keep insisting on the different levels with countries such as indonesia, malaysia and korea, to bring some of their legislation fully in line with the requirements of the sps agreement and of the international standards of the world organisation for animal health. we have asked eu beef businesses to come forward with their specific concerns and to make suggestions on how we might tackle barriers in key markets. it has recently had very positive feedback, and a presentation made by an irish business association will help us in setting priorities and continuing our work.

member of the commission. - the mr president, the environmental damage which may result from the extraction and use of lignite in power stations is one of the issues adequately addressed by community legislation. the mining waste directive requires that plants treating mining waste have a permit, which includes a waste management plan, as well as a plan for the closure and rehabilitation of the plant. these units are required to provide a financial guarantee to cover the cost of restoring the soil. the directive provides for inspections by the competent authorities and includes obligations to prevent pollution of water, air and soil. the directive applies to new installations from may 2008. existing installations must obtain a permit in accordance with the directive before may 2012. member states are also required to draw up by mid-2012 a list of abandoned and decommissioned installations which cause or could cause environmental damage. the european union regulatory framework includes other directives such as the ippc directive and the large combustion plants directive. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. of course, the most important of these is the ippc directive, which requires large combustion plants to have permits based on the application of best available techniques. the large combustion plant directive also sets minimum emission limit values for the most important air pollutants. if an installation ceases to operate, the ippc directive imposes an obligation on the operator to take measures to prevent any pollution risks, as well as landscape restoration measures. this legal framework ensures a high level of environmental protection in the event of potential environmental damage from lignite firing plants. now, as regards the closure of the plants, this will be judged according to whether the plants meet the requirements of the legislation.

countries in the balkans. it is very good that the european parliament is raising this issue so early in the election campaign. it shows how important we all think it is to bring the peoples of the western balkans closer to the european union. this is undoubtedly the most important issue for the citizens of the balkans in their relations with the eu today. visa liberalisation will primarily enable people to move more freely throughout europe and create more open societies. many people in the region - especially young people - have never been to western europe, and a number of opportunities for contacts and exchanges will naturally be created by visa liberalisation. that is the real advantage of this initiative. in 2007, the eu launched a process to end visa requirements for the western balkan countries. this process has two aspects: countries themselves need to make significant progress in document security, better migration legislation, stronger rights for minorities and, not least, the fight against corruption and organised crime. in return, the eu offers visa-free travel. visa facilitation linked to readmission obligations was introduced as early as january 2008. however, only through genuine visa liberalisation will the economic and bureaucratic obstacles resulting from the visa requirement disappear. the liberalisation of visa requirements for citizens of the western balkans is an important measure strengthening the ties between this region and the european union. we can expect that this will stimulate the pro-european orientation of both the governments and the peoples of the region, because it will show that the european integration process has a real tangible advantage. continued isolation, on the other hand, would create a feeling of exclusion and impede the exchange of ideas, and could, in the worst case, dilute narrow-minded nationalism. our aim is, of course, the opposite: to open up the eu, to give countries access to community programmes, to facilitate people-to-people contacts and to promote development and exchanges between the countries of the western balkans and between them and the eu. the visa liberalisation will also create new opportunities for trade, industry and knowledge transfer. these are important elements in mitigating the consequences of the economic crisis. the commission's proposal, presented on 15 july, is therefore very welcome. it proposes that, as a first step, the visa requirement be abolished for citizens of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, montenegro and serbia who hold biometric passports. the aim is to liberalise visa requirements for these citizens by 1 january 2010 and to extend this to other countries as soon as they meet the conditions. the commission's evaluation shows that three countries: serbia, montenegro and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia are largely clear and in principle fulfil the conditions for visa liberalisation. the evaluation of serbia and montenegro is still ongoing and we are awaiting confirmation from the commission in the autumn that all conditions have been met so that we can move forward. i would like to emphasise that many of the conditions we set for liberalisation, such as police reform and the fight against corruption, also favour the countries' preparations for eu membership and thereby create a win-win situation for all of us in terms of harmonising the regulatory framework. it is also a good example of the way in which conditionality works in the western balkans. albania and bosnia-herzegovina will not be covered by this first visa waiver decision, but we are not leaving them in the lurch. i know that many in this house are concerned about this. it is only a matter of time before these countries also meet the necessary conditions of the commission's roadmaps. in order to complete the process as soon as possible, we continue to urge and support albania and bosnia and herzegovina to make further progress on the remaining benchmarks so that they too can hopefully benefit from visa liberalisation in the near future. the eu will do all it can to help and support these two countries in first half of 2008 with the five western balkan countries. roadmaps have been drawn up, setting out criteria for achieving which imply the adoption of structural reforms in the key areas of jha justice, freedom, security. this method has proved to be a very important incentive for the countries of the region to move towards reforms, especially for the security of documents, with the corruption, human trafficking, and finally, of course, fundamental rights, including citizenship issues. after analysing these reports, we can say that the former yugoslav republic of macedonia fulfils all the criteria of its road map. montenegro and serbia have made very significant progress. however, for serbia, conditions remain to be fulfilled, in particular related to the verification of identity documents submitted by residents of kosovo and persons from kosovo residing abroad when applying for a serbian biometric passport. secondly, the border management with kosovo and cooperation with eulex, and thirdly, the development of a national migration strategy. for montenegro, a sustainable solution for the displaced persons is to be defined. measures are still needed to three countries. despite very significant progress in recent months, bosnia and albania have not yet been able to complete the necessary reforms required in the roadmap, such as visa abolition. on the basis of this analysis, the commission, responding to the invitation issued by the general affairs council in june 2009, has therefore proposed the abolition of visas for the citizens of macedonia, montenegro and serbia. for serbia, persons residing in kosovo or persons from kosovo residing abroad who hold a serbian passport issued by a central authority in belgrade shall be excluded from liberalisation and subject to the visa requirement. since 1999, serbia has not been able to verify identity documents for kosovo citizens. the commission has taken into account the security risk posed to the community by this category of persons and the fact that no dialogue on visa liberalisation has yet been launched with kosovo. so the decision to include certain countries in this visa liberalisation is based on the merits of each of the countries individually. for serbia and montenegro, we will be following closely the steps taken by these two countries to ensure that all the criteria are fully implemented. in view of the progress already made by albania and bosnia-herzegovina, the commission is confident that these two countries will be able to meet all the criteria in the near future. in october, their authorities will provide the commission with additional information on the progress made in recent months. on the basis of this information, evaluation missions will be organised early next year and then the commission will draw up further evaluation reports to be discussed with the member states. as a result, the commission hopes to be able to propose visa-free travel in 2010. in accordance with the procedures in force, the proposal will be discussed in the council and the european parliament will deliver its opinion. the formal adoption of the text by the majority of the schengen countries is therefore expected during the swedish presidency, which will allow the effective implementation of visa abolition for the citizens of these three countries from recovery package and the decisions taken in the health check that provide another eur 4.2 billion to face the new challenges, including restructuring in the dairy sector. all this of course is on top other actions for the longer term. if i could start with the report, i will look first at state aid. the report floated the idea that member states could temporarily offer aid of up to eur 15 000 for farmers under this temporary crisis framework. the commission has actually already launched the boat and expects to change the rules in the coming weeks. the second point is streamlining the procedures for responding to prices in the dairy sector. at this moment, milk is not actually included in article 186 of the single common market organisation which allows the commission to take temporary actions quickly under its own power during times of market disturbances. i am therefore proposing that we include the dairy sector in article 186, and this will enable us to spring into action in the future if we hit serious problems in the dairy sector. for example, our recent extension of intervention had to be approved by the council, and parliament voted on this as well, but, if the dairy sector had been included in this article 186, we could have acted immediately. more generally speaking, we could with almost immediate effect mobilise measures stimulating demand and/or we could limit the marketing of milk, and all this would only be put in place on a temporary basis and under the condition that we had the necessary financing available. the third follow-up point from the report concerns the buying-up schemes by member states. one way to restructure is that member states can actually buy quotas from farmers and put these quotas into the national reserve. as you know, the national reserve counts in a sense as part of the member states’ total quota, so if individual producers go over their quota, but member states as a whole do not exceed their quota, with the national reserve included, then no super levy is actually paid. what i intend to propose is that bought-up quota kept within the national reserve will not count as part of the national quota when it comes to deciding whether we have to add or to ask the farmers to pay the super levy or not. if the super levy should then be collected anyway, then the part corresponding to the bought-up quota could then be used for restructuring. it might sound a bit complicated, but it is actually a very efficient tool. all of these steps are actions that we are taking now with an almost immediate impact on the markets, but we also need to do something about steps for the medium and longer term. i would like to thank france and germany here for their ideas and their input on these different possibilities. much better approach than the quota system, and it already works in parts of the european union. milk producers and dairies have clear agreements which remove a lot of the uncertainty. on the other second long-term issue is about the balance of power, and you know that we have had this discussion a lot of times. we need to be able to see within the whole chain from primary producer to member of the commission. − mr president, first of all, let me express my sympathy to the people of taiwan who suffered as result of typhoon morakot and its consequences. the european community mechanism for civil protection made a contribution to the overall relief effort and showed europe’s solidarity with the population of taiwan. on 7 august 2009 taiwan was hit by typhoon morakot, causing major flooding and mudslides. over 150 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced. transport infrastructure, including roads and bridges, was damaged and communication networks were interrupted. around 700 000 homes were left without drinking water. taiwan requested international assistance on 12 august 2009. in response the european commission activated the community civil protection mechanism. the mechanism facilitates and coordinates member states’ in-kind assistance during major emergencies. the european commission deployed a coordination and assessment team to taiwan to assess the needs and to assist the government in its relief efforts. the team undertook several assessment missions to the affected regions, sharing its findings and recommendations with the local authorities and international partners. the mechanism team also facilitated the delivery of in-kind assistance such as water purification equipment donated by sweden and poland, which was delivered to the most affected areas in taiwan. the rapid delivery of this assistance ensured a tangible expression of european solidarity. the presence of the european team on the ground was also received positively. the community civil protection mechanism is a very visible sign of european solidarity with countries worldwide, and i am convinced that it will continue to grow in strength and effectiveness. natural disasters can affect any country in the world. they often carry a heavy human, economic and environmental cost. in the future, climate change makes it likely that we will face acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? we are now at a crucial time. in copenhagen, less than two months from now, the world will reach an agreement to meet the climate challenge. this agreement must meet three conditions: keep global temperature rise below two degrees, cover all countries and adapt future efforts to higher levels of ambition as new knowledge is gained. with 48 days to go until the opening of the major un climate conference, it is high time that political will was translated into concrete action. but the negotiations are going too slowly. several important questions remain to be resolved. many people now choose the very simple to be a business traveler in pessimism. let us be clear: the eu has a different mission! we want the eu to show leadership through a clear and unambiguous political will. for the swedish presidency, a comprehensive and ambitious climate agreement is of the utmost priority. the eu's response to the difficulties in the negotiations is that the pace must be increased. we're going to push to make sure the world reaches the agreement that it needs. we are taking on the challenge of bringing the rest of the world together in an agreement that is sufficient to meet the climate challenge. we are therefore working intensively on two tracks: on the one hand, to send a strong message to our negotiating partners, and on the other, to rally the eu around a strong negotiating mandate for the copenhagen conference. the eu already has a foundation through the climate and energy package agreed by the european parliament and the council in december 2008. i would like to thank in particular the commitment shown by many in this parliament in the work on the climate and energy package. the decision taken by the european parliament at that time gives the eu a strong position in the negotiations. this week, the final pieces of the puzzle are being added to give a complete picture of the strong negotiating position. the negotiations will be concluded at the european council next week and i know that many of you will be following them closely. i am glad that some of you will also have the opportunity to be in copenhagen. i also welcome the resolution which the european parliament is preparing. emissions must be limited to the level required to keep global temperature rise below 2 degrees. that means the offers on the table are not enough. the eu wants to reduce emissions by 30% by 2020, provided that other parties also make sufficient commitments. we see the 30% target as a lever to get others to join us in higher ambitions. by 2050, emissions should be reduced by at least 80%. but to keep warming below 2 degrees, eu action alone is not enough. everybody has to be in it. we have seen some encouraging signals from the new government in japan, for example. we are now calling on other developed countries, not least the united states, to raise their bids. developing countries have the opportunity to achieve sustainable development while reducing emissions. it is about planning for low-emission growth and integrating climate change and adaptation into national development strategies. it is a way of making climate and development policies permeate all policy decisions and ensuring that growth is shared by all, of building and opening up democratic governance, of contributing to gender equality and of combating and reducing poverty. we are making special demands on the fastest growing developing countries, not least china, which is the largest emitter. by 2020, emissions need to be reduced by up to 30% compared to what would have happened without action. development issues must be at the very heart of an agreement in copenhagen. the european council has concluded that climate change is undermining efforts to combat poverty and promote sustainable development. climate change is a threat to the mdgs. development experts will also be involved in the negotiations. we will give particular attention to development issues in the context of the negotiations under way. all countries, except the least developed, should bear the costs of climate change action, but we in the developed countries must show leadership by reducing emissions ourselves and funding important efforts. a viable international framework for cooperation and support to developing countries is needed. such a structure should also help the poorest and most vulnerable countries, which are often the hardest hit by climate change. there are adjustment measures. finally, let me stress that the eu is prepared to take its responsibility. the council is aware of the scale of the funding required. the commission estimates that by 2020 this will amount to some eur 100 billion per year in developing countries. we in the eu are also prepared to provide rapid funding for immediate action as early as 2012 as a way of increasing confidence between north and south in the climate negotiations. we face a great challenge in the final weeks of copenhagen. that's why i'm also turning to you for help. we need leadership from member state governments, action from national parliaments and support from the people of the eu countries. the european parliament has a very important role to play in the work to achieve our goals in copenhagen.
member of the commission. − mr president, let me first of all thank you for giving me the opportunity to express the commission’s views on this sensitive issue. you are already aware that there will be no ambitious deal in copenhagen if the concerns of the developing countries are not taken into account, not only those of emerging countries, but also very much the concerns of the most vulnerable and the poorest developing countries. nevertheless, reaching a good deal in copenhagen is our common interest. developing countries are the most vulnerable countries to climate change. the eu is the first donor in the world and a leader in the fight against climate change. we have to combine our efforts. there is no place for north-south confrontation when you are dealing with climate change. i would even go further and say that no other alliance can be as determining and effective as the one engaging the most vulnerable countries and the ones who have put on the negotiating table the most ambitious proposals to fight this plague – that is to say europe. our general approach towards the most vulnerable countries, followed up to now through the global climate change alliance, is made up of three parallel strands, which are interlinked and are mutually reinforcing. first, building political alliances through reinforced dialogue on climate change. three joint political declarations have been signed respectively with africa, the caribbean and the pacific, plus one with the acp group as a whole. second, promoting sound policies and strategies linking climate change and development. i am of the opinion that climate resilience and low carbon policies must be integrated into wider developments and the poverty reduction strategies of our partners. there can only be a single development strategy, which incorporates climate concerns pursuing the objectives of sustainable development and poverty reduction. it is not a matter of choosing one or the other: both are essential. in this spirit, we already support the implementation of the existing national adaptation programmes of action of ldcs in 15 eligible countries. third, encouraging adequate eu contribution to finance climate actions, in particular for adaptation, which is the priority concern for those countries that are most vulnerable to climate change impact, but that hardly contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. we are only 50 days away from copenhagen. expectations are very high. and we are worried because the negotiations are dangerously close to deadlock at the moment. it is now the time for putting offers on the table. that is what europe has done, and that is what we expect our partners to do as well. firstly, we have made offers in terms of commitments. the eu has already put on the table ambitious targets and commitments – so far the second most ambitious on the table of negotiations. we have already guaranteed a unilateral 20% emission reduction by 2020, and we are committed to increase to 30% if comparable efforts are made by others according to their responsibilities and capabilities. second, offers in terms of financing. we are all conscious that a deal on financing will be crucial to achieving an agreement in copenhagen. to move forward in the negotiations, the ec issued in mid-september its own proposals on finance. one of them is the need for short-term international public funding for climate to be scaled up for the period 2010-2012 to respond as a priority to urgent needs identified in the most vulnerable developing countries and in particular ldcs, sids, and african countries as defined in the bali action plan. another one is the readiness of the eu to take on its fair share of the estimated financing requirements, public funding contributions being based on preferred criteria of ability to pay and responsibility for emissions. this may lead to an eu contribution between eur 2 billion and eur 15 billion annually in 2020. these proposals will be discussed by the european council at the end of october and will hopefully be the basis for a fully-fledged eu negotiation position on finance. but action by the eu alone is not enough. we strongly hope that other developed countries will follow our paths as the pressure grows before copenhagen. we count on developing countries as well. they have to take the opportunity offered by climate financing to fully integrate adaptation into their development strategies and to move gradually to low-carbon development paths for the longer term. although the focus has been up to now on adaptation for the poorest and most vulnerable developing countries, there is some ground to promote the design of low carbon development paths (i.e. mitigation), which are compatible with poverty reduction objectives in those countries. a specific focus on mechanisms to avoid deforestation and promote sustainable management of forests is crucial. indeed, the fight against tropical deforestation is the largest immediate mitigation challenge for the ldcs, and they can be beneficiaries, through mechanisms such as reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation schemes, of its international financing. similarly, ensuring in the future a more balanced distribution of the cdm (clean development mechanisms) investments in favour of the ldcs should also be part of the current reflexion on the reform of this mechanism. finally, a word on the delivery channels for climate funding. we as the commission are not in favour of creating new funds. new funding for climate should use existing and potentially improved delivery channels, promoting a decentralised bottom-up governance structure in support of country-owned actions.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. as you know, the link with the united states and the transatlantic cooperation between the united states and the european union are of great importance. it is a cornerstone of the eu's foreign policy, founded on the values of freedom, democracy and respect for human rights and international law, which is something that unites us. the new administration in the united states has shown great interest in deepening and developing relations between them and us in europe. we have the first transatlantic economic council with president obama's administration on 26-27 october. shortly afterwards, on 3 november, an eu-us summit will take place. these are two important occasions to strengthen our relations. that is why today's debate is very important. i would like to highlight some areas of cooperation in which we hope to achieve results and to deepen our cooperation at the summit. as regards climate issues, we welcome the increased ambition of the united states in this respect. we must work with the us administration to get a comprehensive, globally binding agreement in copenhagen. we call on the united states to set targets comparable to those set by the eu. the united states and the eu must be prepared to jointly support climate action such as emission reduction, adaptation, financing and other support to developing countries. another important issue is, of course, the financial and economic crisis. it will require very close cooperation to follow up the agreements reached at the g20 and to restore confidence in the financial markets. we will work together to ensure that the doha round is successfully concluded in 2010, as it is very important in the work to promote recovery and combat protectionism. of course, we will also discuss a number of regional issues, such as afghanistan, pakistan, iran, the middle east, russia and the western balkans. we have regular and increasingly close cooperation in crisis management, as expressed, among other things, by the us participation in an esdp civilian mission, eulex in kosovo. we also have cooperation on energy issues which now needs to be strengthened, and we hope that we can establish a special energy council between the eu and the us at ministerial level. there is an interest on both sides in deepening cooperation on internal and judicial matters. i shall come back to that in a moment, since i understand that the debates are confused. on non-proliferation and disarmament, cooperation between the eu and the us administration has gained new momentum, and barack obama is making this issue a priority. we hope that this will be reflected in a new joint declaration on non-proliferation and disarmament at the november summit. both sides of the atlantic have an interest in strengthening cooperation in development cooperation. the eu and the us account for the lion's share of the world's total development aid. the forthcoming meeting is therefore an excellent opportunity to discuss this and possible other issues at the very highest level. we are very pleased that the swedish presidency has given us the opportunity to represent the eu. i would also like to say a few words about the economic partnership and the transatlantic economic council, the tec. this gives us a mechanism at the very highest level which can speed up the technical negotiations under way and define new areas of regulatory cooperation. we need to develop a work programme for tec that can be set for next year. it provides us with a forum for cooperation, where we can address issues related to globalisation and rapid technological change. so far this has been an important forum, but it can of course be improved, not least in terms of the broader strategic issues relating to the transatlantic economy and common economic challenges. the transatlantic economic council is becoming increasingly important in the context of the financial crisis. let me now say a few words about judicial and police cooperation. we have been cooperating with the united states in this area for some time, as reflected in a number of extradition and mutual legal assistance agreements which will come into force in a few months' time. we often discuss this with the european parliament, which i know is an active and committed partner in these matters - often a critical partner, which is good. i can only recall in this context the discussions on, for example, passenger name records. the entry into force of the lisbon treaty will deepen the european parliament's influence and involvement in these issues. we are currently working on the so-called washington statement, which will describe the state of play of eu-us cooperation in the field of justice and home affairs. this statement must be meaningful and followed by concrete action. it does not need to be more fancy words, but cooperation must be concrete and operational. we must of course affirm our common values, namely democracy and the rule of law, and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. we are naturally interested in cooperation in all areas which pose a threat to these common values. we seek early consultation between us both when political events occur which may affect the other party. we underline our common ambition to work in international fora to achieve full implementation of multilateral commitments. we are working together to increase the security of travel documents and to introduce biometric passports as an international standard. an important example is the agreement on personal data for air passengers. we will work together to ensure that the agreement works, while protecting privacy and respecting the systems of the different countries. there is a long list of areas of cooperation. let me mention just a few: trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children, drug trafficking, financial crime, cybercrime, corruption, confiscation of proceeds of crime and the proceeds of crime, the fight against terrorism. all this requires joint and to some extent coordinated efforts. we have worked to improve judicial cooperation in the detection, investigation and prosecution of cross-border criminals and terrorists. we look forward to the entry into force of the eu-us extradition and mutual legal assistance agreements early next year. the agreements have now been transposed in all 27 eu countries, and a joint eu-us working group is in place to ensure that they are implemented. seminars are planned to help bring the actors closer together and monitor implementation. in conclusion, let me mention three more points. the first concerns the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. this is extremely important. the fight against cross-border crime and terrorism often requires the exchange of personal data, which to some extent forces us to make concessions in terms of fundamental freedoms and rights. this must be balanced by a basic and strong protection of personal data. cooperation and dialogue in this area continue and should be strengthened. the second point concerns critical infrastructure. we need to work together to address the damage that could be caused to critical infrastructure in the event of a natural disaster or terrorist attack or attacks on our information systems. it could have devastating consequences. there is a great deal of scope for cooperation in this area. thirdly, the eu and the us have committed themselves to working on the basis of the principles of freedom, democracy and justice. we are determined to promote these principles throughout the world. we do this when we work together and also in international forums such as the united nations. the cooperation between liaison officers and delegations has proved fruitful, for example in the western balkans and in afghanistan and pakistan. this cooperation must be improved. the various measures of this cooperation may be complementary. we also need to coordinate our technical assistance better. we will continue donor, aid and operational cooperation in latin america and west africa to help combat drug trafficking and to meet other challenges. i am very pleased that the american administration is showing such great interest in cooperating with us. we have every interest in taking up this invitation to work towards the incorporation of our values and interests in a constructive dialogue which will hopefully lead to concrete results in future cooperation.

prisoners in cuba. this figure has decreased from 2 034 in 2007, but most of the releases were due to completion of sentence. member states’ missions in havana are closely monitoring the list of political prisoners and have a special human rights working group where important cases are discussed. prison conditions, according to human rights defenders and testimonies of political prisoners and their families, are far below the united nations’ standard minimum rules for treatment of prisoners. some prisoners are in very bad health, according to their families, and do not have access to adequate medical care. there have been a number of reports of cruel and degrading retreatment, including beatings of prisoners, denial of appropriate health care and psychological pressure. still, however, there are no reports of prison guards or police being prosecuted for abuse. the cuban government denies the existence of political prisoners and regrettably continues to reject international scrutiny of human rights from independent human rights organisations. the council approach towards cuba was set out in the common position of 1996, which has since been evaluated by the council on an annual basis. in october 2008 the eu and cuba agreed on the resumption of a comprehensive political dialogue. this dialogue, in accordance with eu policies, not only includes the cuban authorities but also civil society and the democratic opposition. the council pays special attention to the principles of democracy, human rights and fundamental freedoms in the 2009 annual evaluation of the common position. in the conclusions from june this year, we made clear that these issues will remain one of the eu’s key priorities in the relationship with cuba. the council particularly urged the cuban government to release unconditionally all political prisoners, including those who were detained in 2003, and we expressed our concerns for the prisoners and their health condition. furthermore the council called upon the cuban authorities to facilitate immediate access of international humanitarian organisations to cuban prisons. since the initiation of the political dialogue with cuba last year, the eu side has brought up the issue of political prisoners at each and every meeting. as stated in the last council conclusions, human rights should always be addressed on these high-level visits and, when appropriate, meetings with the peaceful pro-democracy opposition will be part of these visits. the council decided to pursue the dialogue with cuba because it provides an opportunity to discuss open issues of mutual interest and concern, including the human rights situation, but we remain seriously concerned about the situation in cuba and we will continue to follow individual cases, particularly prisoners with serious health conditions. regarding the particular situation of one of the prisoners mentioned by the honourable member, the european union has made a manifestation of solidarity initiated by the swedish presidency in havana in august. the manifestation was held to show the family of the arrested dr darsi ferrer that the union is concerned that national criminal procedural law is not being observed by the cuban authorities. equally the case of the other prisoner, mr alfredo domínguez, is also being watched by the presidency and raised in the dialogues with cuba, and we do have contact with his family.
